identity.title: Food Safety Plan (Preventive Controls for Human Food): Ready-to-Eat Hummus and Bean Dips, Salem Plant
identity.issuer: Willamette Valley Foods, Inc. (prepared by Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager and PCQI; approved by 'Plant Manager', with no name, signature or date)
identity.site: Salem — 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301

page_refs.agencies: page 7 (section 9, Records, names FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture)

scan.summary: This is the plant's written food safety plan under FDA's preventive controls rule for human food (21 CFR Part 117). It covers the hazard analysis, preventive controls, monitoring, corrective actions, verification, supply-chain, records and training for the refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips made at the Salem plant. It is the core document an FDA or Oregon Department of Agriculture inspector asks for first. The basic structure is sound, but it is missing several parts the rule requires: validation, a recall plan, a reanalysis schedule, a signature, and a full supply-chain program. Several controls are also only partly worked out.
scan.freshness_note: The plan took effect on May 12, 2025, about 16.5 months ago. That is inside the 3-year reanalysis window, which by inference ends around May 12, 2028. The plan does not say when it will be reanalyzed, though. Check whether any product, supplier, equipment or line change since May 2025 should have triggered an earlier update. If a later signed version exists, ask for it. The open gaps from the earlier reading all match this text, so this appears to be the same version that was read before.

gaps.title: No validation of the cook and cooling limits
gaps.description: Nothing shows the cook limit (212°F for 60 minutes) or the cooling limits (135°F to 70°F in 2 hours, then to 41°F in 4 more hours) have been proven to control the hazards. A related problem (inferred): an internal temperature of at least 212°F is at or above the boiling point of water at Salem's elevation. The kettle may not be able to meet this limit reliably. Also, thermometers checked against boiling water at Salem would read slightly below 212°F, so the check itself sits right at the limit.
gaps.fix: Have the PCQI validate both process controls before or soon after use, using scientific studies or literature, or a process authority, with in-plant data. File the validation study with the plan. Consider rewriting the cook limit as a lethality value that can actually be reached (for example, a temperature just below boiling held for a set time). Correct boiling-water calibration for elevation.
gaps.locator: Section 4 (page 4) and section 7 (page 6). Validation is not in the document.
gaps.quote: Minimum 212°F for 60 minutes, measured with a calibrated probe thermometer

gaps.title: Supply-chain program is too thin
gaps.description: The supply-chain section is two sentences. It does not name which hazards the suppliers control (sesame labeling on tahini, Salmonella in tahini, stones in beans). It does not say how suppliers are approved or which verification activity applies to each, and it has no written procedures for receiving. It also does not say who reviews audits or certificates of analysis, or what records are kept.
gaps.fix: Write a Subpart G supply-chain program. Name the hazard each supplier controls, the approval process, the verification activity and how often (onsite audit where a SAHCODHA hazard like Salmonella in tahini applies, unless a written determination says otherwise), how audits and COAs are reviewed, and how receiving is checked. Keep records under 117.475.
gaps.quote: Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot.

gaps.title: No reanalysis schedule or triggers
gaps.description: The plan does not say it will be reanalyzed at least every 3 years. It also does not list the events that require earlier reanalysis: a change in activity, new hazard information, an unanticipated food safety problem, or a preventive control found not to work.
gaps.fix: Add a reanalysis section. Commit to reanalysis at least every 3 years (next by 2028-05-12, inferred from the effective date) and list the triggers. The PCQI does or oversees the reanalysis.

gaps.title: Environmental monitoring procedure is incomplete
gaps.description: The plan gives a count (10 sites, zones 1 and 2) but does not say which locations are sampled, how or when during production, what test and lab are used, or what counts as a positive. Zone 3 is not covered. Quarterly trending is mentioned, but no procedure is given.
gaps.fix: Write an environmental monitoring procedure: site map by zone, number of sites and when they are taken, test organism and method, lab, action limits, and escalation. Link it to the Listeria corrective action already in section 6.
gaps.quote: Listeria spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2

gaps.title: Finished product testing: no procedure and no response to a positive
gaps.description: Monthly Listeria monocytogenes testing is listed, but there is no written procedure covering sampling, number of samples, test method, lab and hold-and-release. There is also no corrective action if a result comes back positive.
gaps.fix: Write a product testing procedure under 117.165(b)(2). Add a corrective action for a positive L. monocytogenes result: hold the lot, evaluate the product, find the root cause, and consider a recall.
gaps.locator: Section 7 (page 6). The corrective action is not in section 6.
gaps.quote: Finished product is tested for Listeria monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory.

gaps.title: No written recall plan
gaps.description: The plan identifies hazards that need preventive controls, so a written recall plan is required. There is none: no steps for notifying customers, public notice, effectiveness checks, or what to do with recalled product.
gaps.fix: Add a recall plan with procedures and assigned responsibility for each of those elements. Include the Oregon, Washington and Idaho retail distribution and lot coding.

gaps.title: Allergen label check at printing and on the line not monitored
gaps.description: The control says labels are reviewed at receipt and at printing, but monitoring covers only receipt. Nothing checks that the right label is on the right product during the run or at changeover.
gaps.fix: Add monitoring of the correct label on the line at start-up, at product changeover and when a new label roll is loaded. Record who checked and when. Add the printing check to monitoring.
gaps.quote: The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs the label log.

gaps.title: Records review leaves out calibration, testing and supplier records
gaps.description: The PCQI's 7-day review covers monitoring records only. Records of thermometer calibration, metal detector service, product testing, environmental monitoring and supplier verification have no review timing. The plan also does not say calibration results are recorded.
gaps.fix: Add review of calibration, product testing, environmental monitoring and supplier verification records within a reasonable time after they are made. Say that calibration results are recorded.
gaps.quote: The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven working days of their creation.

gaps.title: Refrigerated storage hazard has no preventive control
gaps.description: The hazard analysis says growth of Listeria monocytogenes during refrigerated storage needs a preventive control, but section 4 gives none. There is no cooler temperature limit, monitoring or corrective action.
gaps.fix: Add a temperature control for finished-product storage at 41°F or below, with continuous or periodic monitoring, a corrective action for going above the limit, and verification. Support the 45-day shelf life with a challenge study or formulation data.
gaps.locator: Section 3 (page 3). It is missing from sections 4–6.
gaps.quote: Refrigerated RTE product with a 45-day shelf life

gaps.title: Corrective actions skip root cause and product evaluation
gaps.description: Most corrective actions do not say how the problem is fixed at its source, how affected product is evaluated for safety, or how adulterated product is kept out of commerce. Examples: metal detector failure (only re-run), ATP failure, and label mismatch.
gaps.fix: For each control, add: find and correct the cause, lower the chance of it happening again, evaluate all affected product, and prevent adulterated product from entering commerce.
gaps.quote: If the metal detector fails a test piece, all product since the last passing test is re-run through the detector.

gaps.title: Salmonella in ingredients added after the cook step is not analyzed
gaps.description: Tahini, garlic, spices and lemon juice are blended in after the kill step, but the hazard analysis looks at tahini only for sesame. Salmonella in tahini is a known hazard and is not evaluated.
gaps.fix: Add hazard analysis rows for pathogens in each ingredient added after the cook. Choose a control: a supplier-applied control verified through Subpart G, a validated process at the supplier, or another control.
gaps.quote: Cook step is the kill step for the finished product

gaps.title: Stones in dry beans have no working control
gaps.description: The plan says stones are controlled at metal detection. A metal detector does not detect stones (inferred). Supplier screening is named but has no verification.
gaps.fix: Add a control that works for stones, such as a destoner, sorting or inspection step with monitoring. Or make it a supplier-applied control verified under Subpart G.
gaps.quote: Field debris in dry beans, controlled at metal detection and by supplier screening

gaps.title: Plan not signed and dated by the owner, operator or agent in charge
gaps.description: Approval shows only the job title 'Plant Manager'. There is no name, no signature and no date.
gaps.fix: Have the owner, operator or agent in charge sign and date the plan now, and again whenever it is changed.

gaps.title: Chemical hazards other than sesame not evaluated
gaps.description: The hazard analysis does not look at pesticide residues, natural toxins, cleaning and sanitizer chemicals, or allergens other than sesame in the spices and other ingredients.
gaps.fix: Add chemical hazard rows for each ingredient and step, with a justification for each yes or no.

gaps.title: Sesame cross-contact washdown checked only by ATP, and scheduling not monitored
gaps.description: After hummus runs, the washdown is checked with an ATP swab. ATP measures general organic residue, not sesame protein, so a pass does not show sesame has been removed (inferred from how ATP tests work). The rule that hummus runs last, and the washdown itself, have no monitoring record in section 5.
gaps.fix: Add a sesame-specific check (for example, a sesame protein test) after washdown, at least during validation and at set intervals. Add monitoring and records for run order and for completing the washdown before the next product without sesame. Add a corrective action for a failed check.
gaps.quote: washdown verified by ATP swab before the next non-sesame product

gaps.title: No corrective action for unanticipated problems
gaps.description: The plan has corrective actions only for the specific failures it lists. It has nothing for a problem with no set corrective action, or for a preventive control that turns out not to work.
gaps.fix: Add a general procedure: take corrective action, evaluate the product, and decide whether to reanalyze the plan, with records.
gaps.locator: Not in the document (belongs in section 6)

scan.confidence_notes: All seven pages were clear and read in full. What the document is, its date, and the company facts are high confidence. The gaps rely on my knowledge of 21 CFR Part 117 without a fresh check against the eCFR text, so treat the exact section numbers as likely but check them before an inspection. The 14 gaps from the earlier reading all still match this text. I added two new ones: sesame washdown checked only by ATP (partly inferred, based on what ATP tests measure) and no corrective action for unanticipated problems (117.150(b)). The stones gap and the points about the 212°F limit and boiling-water calibration are inferences about how things work, not statements in the document. I cannot tell whether the company is a qualified facility or a very small business, because only production headcount is given and no sales figure. That status could change which Part 117 and Part 121 requirements apply. Deadlines other than the reanalysis date have no calendar dates in the document.

WILLAMETTE VALLEY FOODS, INC.
FOOD SAFETY PLAN
Ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips
Salem Plant, 1850 Fairgrounds Road NE, Salem, Oregon 97301
Effective date: May 12, 2025
Prepared by: Dana Whitfield, Quality Manager, Preventive Controls Qualified Individual
(PCQI certificate, FSPCA course, March 2024)
Approved by: Plant Manager
1. Facility and product description
Willamette Valley Foods produces refrigerated ready-to-eat hummus and bean dips in 8-ounce and 16-
ounce sealed plastic tubs for retail sale in Oregon, Washington and Idaho. The Salem plant operates one
shift, five days a week, with 28 production employees. Products are made from cooked chickpeas or black
beans, tahini, lemon juice, garlic, olive oil, salt and spices, blended, filled, sealed, coded and held
refrigerated at or below 41°F. Shelf life is 45 days refrigerated. Products are labeled with the allergen
statement "Contains: sesame" for all hummus items.
2. Process flow
Receiving of dry beans, tahini and other ingredients → dry storage or refrigerated storage → soaking and
cooking of beans (kettle, 212°F, 60 minutes minimum) → cooling in the blast chiller → blending with
other ingredients → filling and sealing → date coding → metal detection → refrigerated storage →
shipping.
3. Hazard analysis

beans (Salmonella, Listeria monocytogenes) product

4. Preventive controls

Vegetative Cook beans in the kettle to an internal temperature of at Process Minimum 212°F for 60 minutes, measured
pathogens at cook least 212°F for at least 60 minutes with a calibrated probe thermometer
Spore-former Cool cooked beans from 135°F to 70°F within 2 hours Process 135°F to 70°F in 2 hours; 70°F to 41°F in
growth at cooling and to 41°F within a further 4 hours in the blast chiller 4 hours
Listeria in the Sanitation of food-contact surfaces before each Sanitation ATP swab pass before start-up; Listeria
RTE environment production run and between products; environmental spp. swabs, 10 sites weekly, zone 1 and 2
monitoring swabs weekly
Sesame allergen Allergen labeling review for every label at receipt and at Allergen Label matches the formulation sheet;
printing; product scheduling with hummus items last in washdown verified by ATP swab before
the day, followed by full washdown the next non-sesame product
Metal Metal detection of every sealed tub Process Reject at 2.0 mm ferrous, 2.5 mm non-
ferrous, 3.0 mm stainless test pieces
5. Monitoring
The kettle operator records the internal temperature and the time at the start and end of each cook batch
on the cook log. The blast chiller operator records the temperature at 2 hours and at 6 hours on the cooling
log. The sanitation lead records the ATP swab result before each start-up. The line lead runs the three
metal test pieces through the detector at start-up, every two hours, and at the end of the run, and records
the result. The quality technician reviews every label lot against the formulation sheet at receipt and signs
the label log.
6. Corrective actions
If a cook batch does not reach 212°F for 60 minutes, the batch is re-cooked to the critical limit or
discarded, and the cause is recorded. If cooling exceeds the time limits, the batch is discarded. If an ATP
swab fails, the surface is re-cleaned and re-swabbed before production starts. If a Listeria spp. swab is
positive, the site is cleaned and re-swabbed, adjacent sites are added, and product made on that line since
the last negative swab is held pending investigation. If the metal detector fails a test piece, all product
since the last passing test is re-run through the detector. If a label does not match the formulation, the lot
is quarantined and not used. All corrective actions are recorded on the corrective action log and reviewed
by the PCQI within seven days.
7. Verification
The PCQI reviews the cook, cooling, sanitation, allergen and metal detection records within seven
working days of their creation. Probe thermometers are calibrated in ice water and boiling water weekly,
and the metal detector is serviced by the manufacturer annually. Finished product is tested for Listeria
monocytogenes monthly by an accredited laboratory. Environmental monitoring results are trended
quarterly.
8. Supply-chain program
Tahini and dry beans are received only from approved suppliers who provide a current third-party audit
certificate and a certificate of analysis for each lot. The approved supplier list is maintained by the quality
manager.
9. Records
All records named in this plan are kept at the Salem plant for at least two years from the date of the record
and are available to FDA and the Oregon Department of Agriculture on request. Records are reviewed and
signed by the PCQI as described in section 7.
10. Training
All production employees receive food hygiene training at hire and annually. The PCQI holds a current
FSPCA certificate. Sanitation and line leads are trained on the monitoring procedures in this plan.
